analysis.one_liner: Restores victims' right to sue gun makers and sellers for harms from criminal misuse of their weapons.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote in the full three years of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2005, Congress passed a law (the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act) that shields gun and ammunition makers, sellers, importers, dealers, and their trade associations from lawsuits over harms caused when someone criminally or unlawfully misuses a firearm. This bill would repeal those protections, opening the door for victims of gun violence and their families to sue gun companies in federal or state court. It was introduced on January 3, 2019, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would regain the ability to sue gun manufacturers and dealers whose conduct contributed to the harm, and communities bearing the cost of gun crimes. It would also give courts a way to examine industry conduct that current law takes off the table.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the core provisions of the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which bars civil actions and administrative proceedings against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for harms resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.

Reopening that pathway would let victims and their families bring qualified civil liability actions in federal or state court against gun companies, restoring a legal remedy that is currently unavailable to them.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, sellers, and their trade associations, which would lose their broad immunity from civil suits and face potential litigation, litigation costs, and damage awards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations

drawbacks.text: The 2005 law was enacted precisely to protect lawful gun businesses from being held liable in court for the criminal acts of third parties who misuse their products; repealing it would expose companies that followed all laws to lawsuits over conduct they did not commit.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that litigation is an uncertain tool: lawsuits take years, recovery depends on proving specific industry fault, and the threat of suits could raise costs for small licensed dealers rather than directly reduce gun violence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is restoring a civil remedy for people harmed by gun violence that current law denies them, which also creates financial pressure on makers and sellers to change conduct. The cost is borne by the gun industry in litigation exposure, and the bill's critics argue that could sweep in law-abiding businesses and dealers. The bill is narrow — it changes one liability rule and does nothing directly about gun access — so its real-world effect depends heavily on what courts do with the restored ability to sue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for its entire three-year life without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Dwight Evans (D-PA) introduced the Gun Manufacturers Accountability Act in the House on January 3, 2019, the opening day of the 116th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary and then to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained with no further action.
Two House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no further legislative action of any kind was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations remain shielded from civil liability lawsuits, since Congress never considered lifting the protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers, whose liability shield stays

for.name: Rep. Dwight Evans
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's civil liability protections and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 2 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it received.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or floor vote during the entire Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long championed the 2005 liability shield the bill would repeal, and opposed in Congress any effort to reopen gun manufacturers to lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three supporters (the sponsor and two cosponsors) were all House Democrats, and no Republican supported it; with only 3 of 429 House members behind it, opposition was effectively the entire chamber inaction rather than a recorded party split.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, sellers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill would strip away the federal liability shield these businesses have held since 2005, exposing them to civil suits over harms from criminal misuse of firearms. Their interest in keeping the shield runs against gun violence victims, who currently have no such legal remedy.
